newsitem.title: PUERTO RICO: Eleven still missing in Puerto Rican blast.
newsitem.headline: Eleven still missing in Puerto Rican blast.

text.p: Rescue crews worked through the night and into Friday morning clearing debris from around a San Juan shoe store where a devastating blast killed 17 people.

At least 11 people were believed to be buried inside the six-story building, but it was unknown whether they were alive. An engineer said it could be near midday before search teams reached the heart of the building.
The blast, caused by a suspected gas leak, destroyed the side, front and bottom three floors of the building early on Thursday morning in the busy Rio Piedras commercial district of San Juan.

Heavy cranes brought in steel girders on Friday to brace the building, where the top three floors were hanging precariously. Until that work is complete, it will be unsafe for dog teams and other searchers with sensitive probing equipment to go inside, officials said.

"We are getting to the most sensitive parts of the operation right now," said Carlos Pesquera, the secretary of transportation, who is supervising the operation. "We are about to start bracing the building. We expect by about 11:30 a.m. (1530 GMT) to go in."

More than a dozen crushed cars were hauled away from the streets, along with mounds of debris, including chunks of concrete, and twisted metal. Even shoes and Christmas gifts from the ruined shops were cleared in the all-night operation.

The governor's office revised the death toll to 17 from 20, said Areli Escalera, a spokeswoman for the office. One person was in critical condition and not expected to live, about 70 were injured and 11 were missing.

Emergency workers had been forced to halt their search for survivors on Thursday evening, fearing for their own safety until the building could be shored up with steel beams. Faint voices had been heard by some bystanders soon after the explosion, but were not heard later in the day.
Trained search dogs and sophisticated equipment including fiber-optic cameras and listening devices were flown into San Juan by a team of rescue workers from Miami's Metro-Dade fire department.
The Metro-Dade firemen from Miami had begun searching an elevator shaft for victims on Friday morning.

Investigators from the National Transportation Safety Board, which probes U.S. airline accidents, were also dispatched to assist the Puerto Rican government with its investigation into the cause of the accident.
Early indications, and reports that residents had complained of a foul smell prior to the accident, pointed to a possible natural gas leak.

"The owners of the place were complaining that there was a smell for the past two weeks but they (the gas company) hadn't done anything. Today they came and when they were probing, the explosion occurred," police superintendent Pedro Toledo said.

"It is a very unfortunate event that has caused a lot of grief and suffering for families," said Gov. Pedro Rossello. "Our efforts must now be directed to attending to the injured and helping the families of those who died," he said.
